overview: One approach finds the virus itself; the other finds the footprints the immune system left behind after meeting it.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: Methods that detect the virus itself or its components — antigen, nucleic acid, or intact particles.
aspects.valueB: Methods that detect the host's immune response to the virus, typically antibodies, rather than the virus directly.

aspects.label: What Is Actually Measured
aspects.valueA: Viral antigen, viral nucleic acid (RNA/DNA), or visualized virions.
aspects.valueB: Host-produced antibodies (IgM, IgG) specific to the virus.

aspects.label: Timing in the Course of Infection
aspects.valueA: Most useful early, during active infection when the virus is present.
aspects.valueB: Often becomes positive later, after the immune system has had time to mount a response (seroconversion window).

aspects.label: Example Methods
aspects.valueA: PCR/RT-PCR, antigen rapid tests, viral culture, electron microscopy.
aspects.valueB: ELISA for IgM/IgG, neutralization assays, western blot for confirmatory serology.

aspects.label: Typical Clinical Use
aspects.valueB: Confirming past infection or immune status, or diagnosing infections where a direct test window has passed.

aspects.label: Key Limitations
aspects.valueA: Can miss infection outside the window when virus is detectable (e.g. after clearance).
aspects.valueB: Cannot distinguish active current infection from past exposure or vaccination in some cases; window period before seroconversion.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Detects the virus itself, best for acute infection.
aspects.valueB: Detects the antibody response, best for confirming exposure/immune status.
